Hi Chris,

Thanks again for your quick reply.

Thanks for the precision regarding point1 and 2.

Regarding point 3. It seems that the figure didn't upload correctly in the thread, so here's a new shot:

So the trip here is complete (fraction = 1) and semi-variance values at the lower and greater lags are shown. However, there's a gap of about 10 points around the 10th lag, although semi-variance values are in the data frame. Those points are also associated with a DOF < 1. Wishing you a good day, /Phil

> Hi Phil,
>
> Proper CIs on mean UDs are in the short-term pipeline, but I don't know what time constraints you have, so don't wait for me.
> ctmm is currently limited to stationary processes (with the simple exception of non-stationary mean functions), and that will be a longer-term upgrade. So it is a good idea to segment the data into individual behaviors before fitting a stationary model. If I understand what you are doing correctly, there does not need to be a maximum threshold of time between trips. You just want to have the nesting behavior removed.
> If you change the fraction argument of plot.variogram, it can show all of the lags. Alternatively, you can use the slider in zoom().
> Best,
> Chris
>
> On Tuesday, June 30, 2020 at 10:18:25 AM UTC-4, PhilB wrote:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I am working on a central-place foraging species and have a dataset of a few thousand tracks.
> >
> > I am investigating the presence of segregation among the colony's home range. I am then modelling the spatial distribution at the individual-level, for thereafter testing segregation by randomization procedure using the overlap() function (i.e. over colony affiliation of the individuals).
> >
> > Individual tracking was first segmented into foraging trips, in order to reduce the weight of the numerous localization at the colony between the foraging trips. Since the overlap() function doesn't appear to be reliable when implemented with the average distributions (e.g. from mean.UD), I am searching for the most optimal way of aggregating data within the individual stratum. So far, I am considering continuous time between each individual's trip, and by removing the "extra" localisation at the colony (i.e. except the departure and arrival points to the colony). In other words, we have a regular interval of 10 min between every two locations within individuals, having thus a maximum of 10 min at the colony before the next trip.
> >
> > By doing so, and since periodicity is low in the data, the ctmm.fit() give sensible results. However, I am curious to know if another (proper?) way is existing for dealing with such data?
> >
> > Furthermore, I have noticed that sometimes the variograms doesn't show all the lags, although numbers occur in the input data frame. > >
> >
> > Many thanks again, best /Phil

Hi Isabella,

You are running into the same issue that Chris was. Some of your error ellipses have negative variances. Both of you guys are/were using sigloc, so I assume either the issue is with sigloc or with the estimator that sigloc is based on.

For instance, the 3rd individual's 12th time has error ellipse

         x        y
x 37546.68 30190.13
y 30190.13 23520.29

which when fed into eigen() reports

eigen() decomposition
$values
[1] 61527.5030  -460.5261

$vectors
           [,1]       [,2]
[1,] -0.7830312  0.6219824
[2,] -0.6219824 -0.7830312

That second eigenvalue is a variance of -460.5261 square meters, which is impossible.

I suppose there are 3 possible solutions.
Lazy solution: Drop all times with negative variances.
Figure out if there is some way to prevent this in sigloc. Maybe there is a numerical error argument that can be clamped down or something. I'm not familiar with the package.
If this is just numerical error, then you could fix the small, negative eigenvalue to zero, with some code like below. This would be more-or-less correct if the negative variances are just small numerical errors.
If EVD=eigen(COV), then

EVD$vectors %*% diag(EVD$values,2) %*% t(EVD$vectors)

should return back the original COV matrix estimate, and

EVD$vectors %*% diag(pmax(EVD$values,0),2) %*% t(EVD$vectors)

returns a matrix with zero variance substituted for the negative variance, which in this case is

         [,1]     [,2]
[1,] 37724.84 29965.84
[2,] 29965.84 23802.66

and is the same to almost 3 digits.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: An intuitive explanation of AKDE results?
messages.subject_clean: An intuitive explanation of AKDE results?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vilis,

Estimates can be much larger than the data for a couple of reasons:
If the home-range estimates are comparable to other animals, but the sampling period is shorter, then this is probably a data quality issue. The animal wasn't tracked long enough to see it fill out its home range.
If the range estimate is much larger than other animals, but the sampling period is comparable and the model fit still looks good, then the animal probably wasn't resident during the tracking period. If you put tracking data into AKDE where the animal was dispersing, then you get a dispersal range out and not a home range. The KDE is also a dispersal range, but massively biased, because the effective sample size will be ~1, yet KDE is assuming the nominal sample size. The way to think about the dispersal range is to ask how far the animal would travel if it dispersed again, but you don't necessarily assume that the animal will continue to disperse forever. I also would not group or average home-range and dispersal-range estimates together. I'm working on tools for clustering and aggregation right now.
If the fit doesn't look good, with matching asymptotes, then there could be other things happening, and many of those things are the result of the animal not having a stable home range over the entire period of the data. Typically when people estimate home ranges they input tracking data into an estimator that assumes IID data with little regard to whether or not those assumptions are met, and the animal doesn't necessarily have a home range. KDE will not give you any indication that these are not good assumptions.

Best,
Chris

I took an initial guess at the outliers using an initial guess at the RMS UERE (and error model), then obtained a conditionally "good" error model and validated that I would have made the same choice of outliers. I was only removing the very crazy numbers, so there was never any inconsistency.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ingo,

I believe adehabitat's 'ad hoc' bandwidth is Silverman's rule of thumb, which does tend to be too big for IID data, but can actually be too small if the data are very autocorrelated. In general, I do not recommend LSCV bandwidth optimization, even for IID data, because it is slow and unreliable, as you have experienced. MKDE is not really a KDE method, as there is no bandwidth (or anything else) being optimized to minimize the discrepancy between the estimate and the truth, as is the case in KDE. In the 2015 and 2016 Ecology statistical reports, we pointed out that the IID methods like conventional KDE and MCP and the then newer Brownian-bridge based methods are really estimating two different target distributions, which we referred to as range distributions and occurrence distributions. Range distributions quantify the natural variability in the animal's locations, assuming that they continue the same movement behaviors. Occurrence distributions quantify our uncertainty in where the animal was located during the observation period, and limit to zero area when that information is perfect (high sampling rate + low location error = no uncertainty = zero area). So they do become small and patchy as this happens, because they are inherently sampling dependent.

So you first have to decide what distribution you are interested in (space-use prediction versus the unknown realized trajectory) and then choose a good estimator for that target distribution.

Migratory data are very much autocorrelated. They also tend to be very non-stationary. So they violate pretty much every assumption behind conventional KDE. In your turtle example, I see a migration and then a resident period. That's at least two different behaviors, which implies at least two different range distributions that you could potentially estimate. Also, ctmm is currently limited to stationary movement behaviors, so you can only estimate one distribution at a time, anyhow. Inputting multiple behaviors gives you an average behavior, which, in this case, I don't think makes much sense.

I took your turtle data and subset a more resident period with the cleave() function, checked the fit and asymptote, and everything looks okay for that portion of the data (figures attached), though there looked like some additional bi-monthly oscillation that I didn't get into. If you have a lot of turtle migrations to segment, I have heard good things about the segclust2d package.

Now you might also consider the range distribution for the migratory segment, but with only one migration the effective sample size will be ~1. In fact, I got for the fit summary()

$DOF
     mean      area     speed
 1.118727  1.167536 83.811972

The range distribution is trying to predict what future migrations will look like if similar migratory behavior persists, but you can't really estimate variability with a sample size of 1. The result will have massive confidence intervals and is much larger than the data due to severe non-independence. However, you can estimate things like distance and calculate an occurrence distribution, which is basically CIs on the unknown migratory trajectory.

Best,
Chris
